identity.title: Pain abrupt in onset and maximal at onset (thunderclap-type chest/back pain)

technique.how: Ask open-ended how the pain started, then specifically whether it reached its worst intensity within seconds to a minute ('like a switch') versus building over minutes to hours. Record onset character separately from quality (tearing/ripping), location and migration; ask what the patient was doing at onset.
technique.prerequisites: Patient (or witness) able to describe onset; document before analgesia clouds recall.

interpretation.positive_finding: Abrupt, maximal-at-onset pain is present in about 84-96% of confirmed aortic dissections and is a mandated high-risk feature in the AHA aortic dissection detection score; it also fits pneumothorax and PE.
interpretation.negative_finding: Gradual onset makes dissection less likely (RCE pooled LR- 0.3; case-control LR- 0.07) but is not sufficient alone to exclude it given the lethality of a miss.
interpretation.pitfalls: Sensitivity comes largely from case series of confirmed dissection (spectrum bias); patients with syncope, altered mentation or painless dissection cannot report onset. Abrupt onset is common in benign musculoskeletal and anxiety pain, so specificity is low.
interpretation.changes_what: Abrupt onset plus any other ADD-RS high-risk feature: image the aorta (CTA) now; gradual onset with no high-risk features and an alternative diagnosis lowers dissection priority.

estimates.population: Pooled case series of consecutive patients with confirmed dissection (21 studies); finding = pain of sudden onset
estimates.quote: of sudden onset (sensitivity, 84%). The absence of sudden pain onset lowers the likelihood of dissection (negative likelihood ratio [LR], 0.3

estimates.population: Matched case-control: 194 AAD cases vs 776 ED controls with truncal pain <14 days and no clear diagnosis; finding = abrupt-onset pain
estimates.quote: Absence of abrupt-onset pain (sensitivity = 95.9%, negative likelihood ratio = 0.07 [0.03-0.14]) can help rule out AAD

sources.citation: Klompas M. Does this patient have an acute thoracic aortic dissection? JAMA. 2002;287(17):2262-2272.
Ohle R, Um J, Anjum O, et al. High Risk Clinical Features for Acute Aortic Dissection: A Case-Control Study. Acad Emerg Med. 2019;26(3):268-277.
Ohle R, Kareemi HK, Wells G, Perry JJ. Clinical Examination for Acute Aortic Dissection: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Acad Emerg Med. 2018;25(4):397-412.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use gradual onset to exclude dissection in patients with syncope, neurologic deficit, pulse deficit, hypotension, Marfan/known aneurysm, or who cannot give a history.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Abrupt maximal pain with hypotension, focal neurologic deficit, pulse differential or new diastolic murmur is dissection until proven otherwise: CTA and surgical/vascular notification immediately.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Onset descriptors are recall-dependent and were abstracted retrospectively from charts in most source studies; no kappa reported for the finding itself.

extraction_notes: Klompas 2002 RCE sensitivity and LR- come from the abstract (pooled from case series, so specificity/LR+ are not estimable); the CI 0.2-0.5 follows immediately in the abstract but was trimmed from the quote to meet the 25-word limit. Ohle 2019 case-control gives sensitivity and LR- with CI (specificity for abrupt onset not in abstract; case-control design inflates apparent accuracy). The Ohle 2018 meta-analysis abstract does not report abrupt-onset pain (full text not open access), so it is cited for context only, no estimate attached.
